# Consistency

<a id="cns-01"></a>
## CNS-01 - Keep shapes and corner radii consistent

Cards, images, avatars and buttons of the same kind should share shape and corner radius.

- **Source:** PDF 38 (printed 37), 39 (printed 38)
- **Applies when:** Sets of cards and their contents.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Consistency makes elements look and behave alike on one screen and across screens; it helps users learn faster.
- Benefits: ease of use, trust (professional and reliable), reduced cognitive load and a cohesive aesthetic.
- Mixed radii (a square button on one card, a square card and image on another, square avatars on a third) confuse users, look off-brand and lack cohesion.

**Mistake:** Same component type rendered with different corner radii or shapes.  
**Effect:** Looks unpolished and inconsistent.

**Correction:** Standardise radius tokens per component type (e.g. all cards rounded, all avatars circular, all buttons pill).  
**Why it works:** A unified shape language is easier to navigate and pleasing.

**Observable checks:**
- List border-radius values per component type: does any type use more than one?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- Consistency does not mean identical: different backgrounds for product pictures are fine, but essential components (titles, buttons, inputs) must stay consistent.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- 'Consistency' appears in the principles grid (pdf page 6) but has no separate table-of-contents entry; its pages sit inside the Balance and harmony range.

**Related:** [CNS-02](11-consistency.md#cns-02), [BAL-03](10-balance.md#bal-03)

<a id="cns-02"></a>
## CNS-02 - Keep button colours consistent by role

Use one colour scheme for primary and one for secondary buttons everywhere, rather than recolouring buttons per card.

- **Source:** PDF 40 (printed 39), 41 (printed 40)
- **Applies when:** Repeated cards or screens with the same actions.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- A common mistake is using many colours for primary, secondary and tertiary buttons.
- Different button colours make users wonder whether each button has a unique function, divert attention and look off-brand.
- The corrected example uses black for the main button and light grey for the secondary button on every card.

**Mistake:** Each card's buttons recoloured to match its image.  
**Effect:** Users suspect different functions; visual noise.

**Correction:** Map button colour to role (primary/secondary) consistently across all instances.  
**Why it works:** It's obvious what each button does.

**Observable checks:**
- For identical actions across instances, are the button styles identical?
- How many distinct primary-button colours exist on the screen?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [VH-01](02-visual-hierarchy.md#vh-01), [COL-01](14-color.md#col-01)

<a id="cns-03"></a>
## CNS-03 - Put images in consistent containers

When images vary in shape and size, place each in the same container shape (e.g. a circle), then adjust size and position.

- **Source:** PDF 41 (printed 40), 42 (printed 41), 43 (printed 42)
- **Applies when:** Card grids with illustrations or product shots of different shapes.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Varied image shapes and sizes can be unified by placing them inside a consistent shape and adjusting size and position.
- Images with different shapes, sizes and positions look disconnected, without unity or flow.

**Mistake:** Raw images of differing sizes and positions in otherwise identical cards.  
**Effect:** Disconnected look; content starts at different heights.

**Correction:** Same-size tinted circle (or other fixed container) in the same spot on each card.  
**Why it works:** The container creates uniformity even when the image content varies.

**Observable checks:**
- Across sibling cards, are image boxes the same size and position?
- Does text start at the same vertical position in each card?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [CNS-04](11-consistency.md#cns-04), [BT-02](19-content-and-states.md#bt-02)

<a id="cns-04"></a>
## CNS-04 - Keep card heights equal and CTAs aligned

With three or more cards in a row, give them the same height; edit copy to equal line counts, or fix heights and bottom-align the CTAs.

- **Source:** PDF 43 (printed 42), 44 (printed 43)
- **Applies when:** Rows of cards with variable-length titles or descriptions.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- With three or more cards, keep them the same height; keep headings and descriptions about the same length, ideally the same number of lines if you can influence the copy.
- If you can't control the copy, make all cards the same height and align the CTA buttons at the bottom, leaving extra space in the middle to give an illusion of uniformity.

**Mistake:** Cards whose heights and CTA positions vary with copy length.  
**Effect:** Ragged row; CTAs at different heights.

**Correction:** Equalise copy length, or use equal-height cards with bottom-aligned CTAs.  
**Why it works:** Uniform rows look orderly and CTAs are easy to find.

**Observable checks:**
- In a card row, do card bottoms align? Do CTA buttons share the same y?
- In CSS: is the card a flex column with the CTA pushed to the bottom (e.g. margin-top:auto)?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [CNS-03](11-consistency.md#cns-03), [ALN-02](05-alignment.md#aln-02)

<a id="cns-05"></a>
## CNS-05 - Use one icon style; vary style only to signal state

Don't mix simple and detailed or outline and filled icons on one screen; choose a set and stick to it. Mixing filled/outline is fine to mark the selected item.

- **Source:** PDF 45 (printed 44), 46 (printed 45)
- **Applies when:** Icon usage across lists, navigation and toolbars.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- A common error is mixing icon sizes and types (simple vs detailed, outlined vs filled) on the same screen; decide the style ahead and keep it across screens.
- Exception: mixing styles to indicate states, e.g. a filled icon for the selected bottom-nav tab and outlined icons for the rest, serves a functional purpose.
- A custom set or open-source icons are fine, but the set should match the brand image and you shouldn't mix two sets with different properties.

**Mistake:** A list mixing a detailed user icon, bold search, filled heart, filled share and filled bell at different sizes.  
**Effect:** Inconsistent, unprofessional look.

**Correction:** Use a single outlined, same-weight, same-size set with aligned labels.  
**Why it works:** Uniform icons read as one system.

**Observable checks:**
- Do icons on the screen share stroke weight, fill style, size and source set?
- Is any filled/outline mixing explained by a selected or active state?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- Filled vs outlined to show selected vs unselected state (e.g. bottom navigation).

**Related:** [ALN-02](05-alignment.md#aln-02), [NAV-01](19-content-and-states.md#nav-01)
